label: lem:translations
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Finite-translation product estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
Take $a_0$ small enough that the Fourier support of every $Ef_j$ is strictly inside the frequency cube $(-\pi/a_0,\pi/a_0)^{n+1}$. Choose a smooth cutoff supported in this cube and equal to one near these supports, and let $\psi_0$ be its inverse Fourier transform. Poisson summation gives the oversampled reconstruction formula
\[
 Ef_j(z)=a_0^{n+1}\sum_{v\in a_0\mathbb Z^{n+1}}
                 Ef_j(x+v)\psi_0(z-x-v).
\]
The series converges absolutely, since $Ef_j$ is bounded and $\psi_0$ is Schwartz. Consequently, for every $s>0$, uniformly in $x\in B$,
\[
 \sup_{z\in B}|Ef_j(z)|^s
 \lesssim_s\sum_{\substack{v\in a_0\mathbb Z^{n+1}\\|v|\lesssim K^2}}
 |Ef_j(x+v)|^s+\operatorname{RapDec}(R)\left\lVert f_j\right\rVert_{2}^s.
\]
For $s\le1$, use subadditivity; for $s>1$, use weighted H\"older. The omitted lattice tail has arbitrary decay in $K$, hence in $R$ after choosing the Schwartz order.

Apply this with $s=q/k$, multiply over $j$, and integrate over $x\in B$. Using $\left\lVert Ef_j\right\rVert_{L^r(B)}\le|B|^{1/r}\sup_B|Ef_j|$, we bound the $q$-th power of the left side of \eqref{eq:translation-product} by $K^{O(1)}$ times
\[
 \sum_{v_1,\ldots,v_k}\int_B
             \prod_{j=1}^k|Ef_j(x+v_j)|^{q/k}\,d x
\]
and a negligible error. Selecting a largest term proves the lemma, including $r=\infty$.

label: eq:jacobi-four-squares
title: Proof
body_md:
For odd $N$, Jacobi's identity gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jacobi-four-squares}
 r_4(N)=8\sum_{a\mid N}a\ge8N,
\end{equation}
where ordered representations with signs are counted; see \cite[Section 27.13(iv)]{DLMF}.
Choose an odd $b\in[5Q/4,3Q/2]$ and
\[
 z\in(2\mathbb Z)^{d-4}\cap B(0,Q/10).
\]
Then $N=b^2-|z|^2$ is odd and comparable to $Q^2$. There are $\gtrsim Q^2$ vectors $a\in\mathbb Z^4$ with $|a|^2=N$, and $h=(a,z)$ satisfies $|h|^2=b^2$. There are $\sim Q$ choices of $b$ and $\sim Q^{d-4}$ choices of $z$, including the unique empty vector when $d=4$. We obtain $\gtrsim Q^{d-1}$ distinct pairs. Retain a subset of cardinality comparable to $Q^{d-1}$; no upper estimate for the full representation count is needed.
